In this notebook, you are going to do a preliminary analysis on the Swiss population, that will then allow you to answer the following questions:

> "How has the population in Swiss cantons changed in the past 10 years?"
>
> "Are swiss residents living in big or small households?".

To best answer these questions, we have downloaded data made available by [FSO](https://www.bfs.admin.ch/bfs/en/home/statistics/population.html) and have reshaped them for you to work with during this workshop.

You can find the data in the `data` folder of `workshop-content`. From this notebook, its path is `../data/`.

The following exercises have been designed to allow you to apply what you learn in the workshop to a real-world dataset.

## Exercise 1

::: callout-important
This Exercise comes after the first topic: **Data Import**
:::

### Attach the Packages

Attach the Packages that you have seen so far.

::: callout-tip
## Hint

Take a look at the format of the data first, so you can decide which Packages you need to attach them.
:::

```{r}
library(readr) # to import text files
library(readxl) # to import excel files
library(dplyr) # to wrangle the data
library(visdat) # to visualise the data structure
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)
library(ggplot2)
```

### Import the data

Now load all datasets:

-   `communes_population.csv`
-   `communes_ids.xlsx`
-   `district_ids.csv`

::: callout-tip
Assign the contents to the tables `communes_population`, `communes_ids`, `district_ids`, respectively.
:::

```{r}
## load the communes_population
communes_population <- read_csv("../data/communes_population.csv")

## load the communes ids
communes_ids <- read_excel("../data/communes_ids.xlsx", 
    sheet = "communes_ids", skip = 2)

## load the district ids
district_ids <- read_csv("../data/district_ids.csv")
```

## Exercise 2

::: callout-important
This Exercise comes after **Section 1 (Subsections 1.1-1.5)** of the second topic: **Data Wrangling**
:::

### Explore the data

Now take a look at the imported data and make sure all the numeric and non-numeric columns have been imported correctly.

To do so, you can use different functions: `slice_head()`, `glimpse()`, `vis_dat()`. You can also click on the blue arrow in the `Environment` tab.

```{r}
library(dplyr)
slice_head(communes_population, n = 5)
```

```{r}
library(visdat)
vis_dat(communes_population)
```

```{r}
glimpse(communes_ids)
```

### How many communes are included in the dataset?

::: callout-tip
You can count the rows of the `communes_ids` dataset.
:::

```{r}
communes_ids %>% 
  nrow()
```

### How many inhabitants were living in a 4 people household in the commune of "1123 Altishofen" in 2013? Use code to find out.

```{r}
communes_population %>% 
  filter(commune == "1123 Altishofen", household_size == "4 Personen") %>% 
  select(x2013) # maybe call the columns are "year"
```

### In how many communes has the population decreased in 1 Person households between 2012 and 2021?

::: callout-tip
1- Keep only the "1 Person" household sizes

2- Calculate the difference between the population registered in 2021 and 2012

3- Keep only the rows for which the calculated difference is lower than 0

4- Count the rows: this is your answer

5- Optional: keep only the relevant columns

6- Optional: arrange by the difference you calculated
:::

```{r}
communes_decreased <- communes_population %>% 
  filter(household_size == "1 Person") %>% 
  mutate(difference = x2021 - x2012) %>% 
  filter(difference < 0) %>% 
  select(commune, difference, x2012, x2021) %>% 
  arrange(difference)

communes_decreased

communes_decreased %>% 
  nrow()
```

The population living in 1 Person households has decreased in `r nrow(communes_decreased)` communes.

## Exercise 3

::: callout-important
This Exercise comes after **Section 1 (Subsections 1.7-1.9)** of the second topic: **Data Wrangling**
:::

### Which is the canton with the highest number of districts?

::: callout-tip
Use `group_by()` and `summarise()`. Group the data by canton then compute the number of districts. Print only the canton that has the most districts.
:::

```{r}
district_ids %>% 
  group_by(canton) %>% 
  summarise(number_of_districts = n()) %>% 
  ungroup() %>% 
  arrange(desc(number_of_districts)) %>% 
  slice_head(n=1) #optional
```

## Exercise 4

::: callout-important
This Exercise comes after **Section 2** of the second topic: **Data Wrangling**
:::

### Calculate the total population in 2021 by district.

::: callout-tip
Find a way to join together the `communes_ids` and `communes_population` data sets first. Then use `group_by()` and `summarise()` to compute the population of each district in 2021 (sum the population of all communes in each district)
:::

```{r}
communes_population %>% 
  left_join(communes_ids, by = "commune") %>% 
  group_by(district) %>% 
  summarise(population = sum(`x2021`))
  

```

## Exercise 5

::: callout-important
This Exercise comes after **Section 3** of the second topic: **Data Wrangling**
:::

::: callout-warning
Here you will use the `{tidyr}` library. Remember to load it!
:::

### Transform the `communes_population` to long format

::: callout-tip
Create a `communes_long` by transforming the `communes_population` to longer format (use `pivot_longer()`).
:::

```{r}
communes_long <- communes_population %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = x2012:x2021, 
               names_to = "year", 
               values_to = "population") 
  
```

### Summarise the data by canton and by year

Create a new tibble called `canton_population`, which is the summarised version of `communes_long`.

1- You can see that you are missing the "canton" information in the `communes_long`, find a way to join `district_ids` and `communes_ids` to `communes_long`.

```{r}
communes_long <- communes_long %>% 
  left_join(communes_ids, by = "commune") %>% 
  left_join(district_ids, by = "district")

communes_long
```

2- Now create the tibble `canton_population` by grouping by `canton` and `year`, and summarising the data by canton. (The population of a canton is the sum of the population of each commune comprised in it).

```{r}
canton_population <- communes_long %>% 
  group_by(canton, year) %>% 
  summarise(population = sum(population), .groups = "drop")

canton_population
```

## Exercise 6

::: callout-important
This Exercise comes after the last topic: **Data Visualisation**
:::

::: callout-warning
Here you will use the `{ggplot2}` and the `{stringr}` libraries. Remember to attach them!
:::

Clean the `year` column by removing the `x` in the `canton_population` tibble that you have created before.

- You can use `str_remove()` function to remove the "x".

- The resulting variable will be of type "character": change it to numeric.

See the example below:

```{r eval = FALSE}

library(stringr)

my_data <- my_data %>% 
  mutate(var_cleaned = str_remove(var_to_clean, "x")) %>% 
  mutate(var_cleaned = as.numeric(var_cleaned))
```

```{r}
canton_population <- canton_population %>% 
  mutate(year = as.numeric(str_remove(year, "x")) )
```

### Show the evolution of the population by canton.

To do so, draw a line per canton by mapping the `color` to the canton.

::: callout-tip
Map the `year` to the `x` and the `population` to the `y`. Use `geom_line()`.
:::

```{r}
canton_population %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = population, color = canton)) +
  geom_line() 
```

### Compare the population between 2012 and 2021 for the different cantons.

Create a horizontal bar blot, mapping the `fill` to the year so you have two separate bars, one for each year. In order to avoid stacking the bars on top of each other (the default in `{ggplot2}`), you can add the argument `position = "dodge"` to the `geom_col()`.

```{r}
# subsetting the data, so we have only years 2012 and 2021
canton_population %>% 
  filter(year %in% c(2012, 2021)) %>% 
  # transforming the years as characters, to have a discrete palette
  mutate(year = as.character(year)) %>% 
  # building the plot
  ggplot(aes(y = canton, x = population, fill = year)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge")
```

### Create a plot per canton

```{r}
canton_population %>% 
  filter(year %in% c(2012, 2021)) %>% 
  mutate(year = as.character(year)) %>% 
  ggplot(aes(y = population, x= year, fill = year)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  facet_wrap(vars(canton), scales = "free_y")
```

### Optional: Use a different theme

Apply a different theme to the previous plots.

::: callout-tip
If you write `theme_` in the console, all the preset themes will appear in a drop down menu. A good choice is usually `theme_minimal()` for a more minimal look.
:::

Set the `height` and the `width` so that the plot is readable.

